record.paper_title: Open questions in massive star research
record.original_question: How efficient is mass transfer in close massive binaries, meaning what fraction of mass lost by the donor is retained by the accretor rather than immediately ejected or lost from the system? The open problem is to find a physical prescription for mass-transfer efficiency that explains why some systems evolve nearly conservatively while others evolve highly non-conservatively, and that captures the strong dependence on binary properties and stellar mass rather than assuming one constant efficiency for all systems.

evidence.quote: This is problematic because we know that some binary systems evolved through mass transfer rather conservatively while other did not.
A refined mass transfer scheme which accounts for the strong mass dependence of the mass transfer efficiency appears therefore warranted.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a close binary star system consisting of two massive stars (with zero-age main-sequence masses typically ≳ 8 solar masses) in orbit close enough that, during their evolution, the more evolved component (the donor) overflows its Roche lobe and transfers mass to its companion (the accretor). Define the mass-transfer efficiency β as the fraction of the mass lost by the donor that is actually accreted and retained by the accretor, with the remaining fraction 1 − β being ejected from the system (carrying away mass, energy, and angular momentum). 

Empirical evidence from observed post–mass-transfer binaries indicates that β is not a universal constant: some systems appear to have evolved nearly conservatively (β close to 1), while others have evolved highly non-conservatively (β close to 0), and the efficiency seems to depend strongly on binary parameters such as component masses, mass ratio, orbital period, and evolutionary state at the onset of Roche-lobe overflow.

Problem. Derive, from first physical principles governing Roche-lobe overflow, accretion onto a rotating star, radiation pressure, tidal interaction, and angular-momentum transport, a predictive prescription
  β = β(M_donor, M_accretor, P_orb, evolutionary state, …)
that (i) reproduces the observed dichotomy between near-conservative and highly non-conservative evolution in close massive binaries, and (ii) captures the strong dependence of mass-transfer efficiency on stellar mass and binary configuration, rather than treating β as a single constant for all systems.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent 2024 studies in Astronomy & Astrophysics still treat mass-transfer efficiency as a free parameter and explore grids of constant values, with observational constraints from SMC eclipsing binaries indicating no single efficiency reproduces all observed populations (high β ≳ 50% needed for Be/X-ray binaries; low β ∼ 10% needed for Wolf-Rayet star counts). No accepted first-principles prescription β(M, q, P_orb, ...) has been established, indicating the problem remains open.

status_evidence.snippet: prescription for the boundary between stable mass transfer and L2 overflow for arbitrary accretion efficiencies ... grids of binary models adopting various constant mass-transfer efficiencies
status_evidence.claim: Recent work still parametrizes mass-transfer efficiency as a constant input rather than deriving it from first principles.

status_evidence.title: Efficiency of mass transfer in massive close binaries — SMC eclipsing binaries
status_evidence.snippet: observed populations cannot be reproduced with a single mass-transfer efficiency
status_evidence.claim: Empirically a single global β fails; efficiency varies with system properties.

status_evidence.title: Analytic approximations for massive close post-mass transfer binary systems
status_evidence.snippet: the initial mass ratio and the mass-transfer efficiency of the binary have little impact on the outcome of Case A mass transfer
status_evidence.claim: Mass-transfer efficiency remains treated as a free input in 2024 analytic models.
